description: Wir entwickeln Missionsplanungstool für die CLPS Lunar Challenge. Am lunaren Südpol führen extreme Lichtverhältnisse und flache Winkel zu massiven Kraterschatten. Diese trennen Rover sofort von Solarenergie und der direkten Funkverbindung zur Erde – selbst bei kurzen Distanzen. Unser Tool nutzt präzise Höhendaten, um im Voraus optimale Fahrtrouten sowie strategische Standorte für Kommunikationsrelais zu berechnen .
summary:
Our project, Moon Landing Site Navigator, is an interactive web application designed to help users explore and compare potential landing locations on the Moon.

Choosing a suitable landing site is an important challenge for future lunar missions. Factors such as sunlight, communication with Earth, and surface conditions must be considered.

To address this challenge, we developed a website featuring interactive 2D maps, a rotatable 3D Moon, and five prototype landing locations. Our application can retrieve NASA/JPL Horizons data to analyze sunlight and Earth visibility across different time periods.

We also integrated an AI assistant to help users understand the information and explore the results. Additional features include data visualization, location comparisons, and CSV export.

Some scientific parameters currently use clearly labeled demonstration data rather than verified NASA measurements.

Our goal is to make lunar exploration more accessible, educational, and understandable while demonstrating how space data and modern web technologies can support preliminary mission planning.
details:
Moon Landing Site Navigator – Project Details

What does our project do?

Moon Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web application that helps users explore and compare potential landing sites on the Moon.

Finding a suitable landing location is challenging because future lunar missions need to consider sunlight, communication with Earth, terrain conditions, and possible hazards.

Our website provides interactive 2D lunar maps and a rotatable 3D Moon. Users can explore five prototype locations, select different sites, and compare their displayed characteristics.

How does it work?

Our application can retrieve astronomical data from NASA/JPL Horizons to calculate and visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to selected lunar locations.

Users can explore different time periods, including 24 hours, 3 days, and 7 days, to examine sunlight and Earth visibility conditions.

The website also includes an AI assistant powered by Groq that can answer questions and help users understand the displayed information.

We developed a multilingual interface supporting English, German, and Spanish to make the application more accessible to international users.

Additional features include data visualization, CSV export, and an experimental local machine-learning score.

Technologies we used

We developed the project using:

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive website.
  • WebGL for the 3D Moon visualization.
  • Python for supporting data-processing tools.
  • NASA/JPL Horizons for astronomical position data.
  • NASA lunar imagery for visual references.
  • Cloudflare Workers for backend API communication.
  • Groq AI for the conversational assistant.

What makes our project creative?

Our project combines lunar visualization, astronomical data, interactive comparisons, and artificial intelligence in one accessible platform.

Instead of presenting complex scientific information only as numerical tables, we allow users to explore lunar locations visually and compare different conditions.

Benefits and intended impact

Our goal is to make lunar exploration easier to understand for students, researchers, and space enthusiasts.

The application demonstrates how publicly available space data and modern web technologies can support education and early-stage mission planning concepts.

Scientific transparency

Our project is currently an educational prototype, not a validated landing-safety system.

Some parameters, including ice estimates, slope, temperature, hazard overlays, and the experimental machine-learning score, use clearly labeled demonstration data rather than verified NASA measurements.

Our current visibility analysis also does not account for detailed local terrain obstruction.

In future development, we would like to integrate validated lunar terrain datasets and improve the scientific accuracy of landing-site comparisons.
